Izabel, welcome. You are on this stage with a client who very nearly fired you. Let us start there. How bad was it?
Never had we lost a client's confidence that fast, Marcus. One week. That is my hook, and I am not going to soften it.
Most companies would frame that quarter rather differently on a stage like this one.
Most would. Not only did we publish the numbers, we published the ugly ones — the month we lost two accounts.
And you brought David Chen with you, which buys you a great deal of credibility in this room. What actually changed for him?
One thing. Only after the weekly report started did his warehouse start trusting us again. The dashboard did not win him back; the honesty did.
We have four minutes before I open the floor, and this room does ask hard questions. Is there anything you would rather not be asked?
Nothing at all. Rarely does a supplier get to answer in public, so I would rather field a hard question off the cuff than deliver a safe answer I rehearsed on the plane.
At no point did we ask them to keep the failure quiet.
Rarely does a supplier get to answer in public, so I will.

Izabel, it is David Chen. I am at the airport, boarding in twenty minutes, so listen rather than call back. I have been thinking about how we split this on stage. You take the failure. I take the recovery. That order matters, because if I open with how good the fix was, nobody in that room believes me, and rightly so. Here is what I am going to say when the moderator turns to me. I am going to say that at no point did AVRT ask us to keep the failure quiet, and that never in eleven years of buying components had I seen a supplier publish a number that made it look worse. That is the whole reason I agreed to sit next to you. One warning, though. There is a purchasing director from Ohio in the front row who will ask you what it cost. Do not dodge it. Give her the eleven months and let her do the math herself. And Izabel, please do not read from your notes. Rehearse it tonight, then leave the paper in the hotel room.

Good morning, Izabel. Sofia here with the run of show for tomorrow. Your panel is at eleven fifteen, right after the keynote, in the main hall. Forty minutes total: twenty-five with the moderator, fifteen for questions from the floor. The moderator is Marcus Hale, and he sent me his three questions in advance, which is unusual and very helpful. One, how bad was it. Two, why publish the numbers instead of the apology. Three, what you would tell a room full of suppliers who are afraid of the same thing. Two practical notes from the production team. There is no lectern, so you will be on a stool with a handheld microphone, which means no notes and no slides. And they record everything, so whatever you say becomes a clip. My advice is to decide your one line before you walk on, the line you would be happy to see quoted out of context, because that is exactly what will happen. I have booked the room at nine tonight if you want to rehearse it out loud with me.
